name: AIDA
description: Attention → Interest → Desire → Action. Classic funnel structure.
example: Hook: shocking stat (Attention). Expand with context (Interest). Show benefit of solving it (Desire). Ask reader to try it (Action).

name: PAS
description: Problem → Agitate → Solve. Name the pain then offer relief.
example: Name a PM struggle (Problem). Show how it gets worse if ignored (Agitate). Share your framework to fix it (Solve).

name: Before-After-Bridge
description: Show the before state and after state then bridge the gap.
example: Before: chaos in stakeholder meetings. After: aligned in 15 mins. Bridge: here's the 3-step process I use.

name: Star-Story-Solution
description: Introduce a character face a challenge and share the solution.
example: Star: me as a new PM. Story: first feature launch flopped. Solution: the user research habit I built.

name: Hero-Journey-Mini
description: Condensed hero's journey — ordinary world crisis transformation return.
example: Normal PM life → crisis moment in a launch → lesson learned → new normal with growth.

name: SCR
description: Situation → Complication → Resolution. Consulting-style structure.
example: Situation: company growing fast. Complication: PM team can't keep up. Resolution: the hiring framework we built.

name: Three-Act
description: Setup → Confrontation → Resolution. Classic story arc.
example: Act 1: got the job at Amex. Act 2: imposter syndrome hit hard. Act 3: what helped me push through.

name: Inverted-Pyramid
description: Lead with the conclusion then provide supporting details.
example: Key insight first: 'customer calls beat surveys every time.' Then share 3 reasons why with examples.

name: Chronological
description: Events told in the order they happened. Simple and clear.
example: Month 1 at Amex: confused. Month 6: finding my feet. Month 12: leading my first initiative. Month 36: here's what I know now.

name: Compare-Contrast
description: Put two things side by side and draw conclusions.
example: Good PM vs great PM. Same meeting same problem. Completely different approaches. Here's what separates them.

name: Cause-Effect
description: Show how one thing led to another in a chain.
example: Skipped user research → built wrong feature → wasted 2 sprints → learned the hard way that discovery isn't optional.

name: Question-Answer
description: Pose a question then systematically answer it.
example: How do you say no to your CEO? Here are 4 ways I've done it without getting fired.

name: Tutorial-Steps
description: Numbered step-by-step instructions.
example: Step 1: Book 3 customer calls. Step 2: Ask open-ended questions. Step 3: Map answers to your roadmap. Step 4: Present findings.

name: Listicle-Narrative
description: Numbered list where each item has a mini-story or insight.
example: 5 things IIT Delhi taught me that have nothing to do with engineering. Each point is a short story from college.

name: Problem-Insight-Action
description: State a problem share a non-obvious insight then give one action.
example: Problem: PMs waste hours in alignment meetings. Insight: most misalignment is about vocabulary not strategy. Action: start every meeting by defining 3 key terms.

name: Tension-Release
description: Build tension through the post then release it with the payoff.
example: Build up the stress of a product launch going wrong. Escalate with each paragraph. Release with the unexpected save and lesson.

name: Bookend
description: Start and end with the same image/phrase creating a satisfying loop.
example: Open: 'Nobody told me being a PM would be lonely.' Close: 'So I'm telling you. Being a PM can be lonely. And that's okay.'

name: Pyramid-Stack
description: Start with the smallest detail and build to the big picture.
example: One Slack message → one misunderstanding → one missed deadline → one failed launch. Small things compound.

name: Myth-Reality
description: State the myth then reveal the reality with evidence.
example: Myth: PMs need to be technical. Reality: PMs need to ask the right questions. Here's proof from my last 5 projects.

name: Letter-Format
description: Write as a letter to someone — past self future self or a persona.
example: Dear 22-year-old me — you're about to choose between PWC and a startup. Here's what I wish you knew.

name: Sandwich
description: Positive → Negative/Hard truth → Positive. Easy to digest structure.
example: The best part of being a PM (autonomy). The worst part (blame without authority). Why I'd still choose it every time.

name: Rule-of-Three
description: Three points/stories/lessons. Simple and memorable.
example: 3 rules I follow in every stakeholder meeting: 1) Listen first. 2) Repeat back. 3) Commit to one action.

name: Dialogue-Driven
description: Tell the story through actual conversations and quotes.
example: My manager: 'Why did you build this?' Me: 'The stakeholder asked for it.' Manager: 'Since when do stakeholders write PRDs?'

name: Parallel-Structure
description: Two stories running side by side that connect at the end.
example: Story A: a PM who always says yes. Story B: a PM who always asks why. Where they both end up 2 years later.

name: Gap-Analysis
description: Show where you are vs where you should be and how to close the gap.
example: Where most PMs are: reactive firefighters. Where they should be: proactive strategists. The 3 habits that close the gap.

name: Confession-to-Lesson
description: Start vulnerable with a mistake then extract the lesson.
example: I once shipped a feature without any data backing. It flopped. Here's the data checklist I use now before every launch.

name: Reverse-Chronology
description: Start from the outcome and work backwards to the origin.
example: Today I lead product at Amex. Rewind 3 years: I couldn't even write a user story. Here's every step in between.

name: Rapid-Fire
description: Quick succession of short punchy statements building momentum.
example: Ship fast. Talk to users. Kill your darlings. Say no more. Write better PRDs. Read more. Sleep enough. Repeat.

name: Unexpected-Turn
description: Build the story in one direction then pivot to a surprise ending.
example: Everyone expected the feature to fail. The data looked terrible. The team was nervous. And then... it became our #1 growth driver.

name: Framework-Breakdown
description: Present a framework visually then explain each component.
example: My 3C framework for PM decisions: Context (what's happening) → Constraints (what limits us) → Choice (what we do). Here's how each works.

name: Escalation
description: Each paragraph raises the stakes higher than the last.
example: First it was a small bug. Then a customer complaint. Then 10 complaints. Then the CEO's email. Here's how we handled it.

name: Socratic
description: Guide the reader through questions that lead to your conclusion.
example: What if I told you standups don't improve velocity? What if the data proves it? What would you change? Here's what I changed.
